blocks.p: The Mercy Office had built its house on Serenity because nothing on Serenity ever made a sound.

The colony lay deep in the ice of Europa, a honeycomb of warm chambers cut out of an old frozen sea, and the ice took every noise and swallowed it. Footsteps went soft. Voices went soft. Even the machinery that kept the chambers warm gave off no more than a hum that you felt in your teeth rather than heard. Visitors from Abundance spoke of the silence the way people speak of a cold: something that got into you and took a few days to get out.
Sol had always liked it.

They had made the crossing in the night. He had lain down in the stasis pod at the Abundance port with the chill coming up through the cushion and Pell settling into the next pod with a small sigh of contentment, and the last thing he felt was the Halo’s pulse at his temple, faint and steady as a second heartbeat. Then nothing. Then the pulse again, quickening, and warmth in his fingers, and the lid lifting on a blue light that was not Mars. By the clocks of the worlds the crossing took no time at all. The gravity drive folded the distance shut and let it go, and the ship was simply elsewhere. But the body kept its own clock, and by that clock the fold took five hours: five hours of a strain no waking body had ever survived, which was why every soul crossed asleep. The stasis made those hours nothing too. What took time was the running out, on ordinary thrust, until a world’s pull was thin enough to light the drive, and the running in at the other end. He had made it more times than he could remember, and he had never once dreamed.

Serenity’s port opened onto the Long Gallery, which ran through the ice to the colony’s heart, and the gallery was lit from above by the lanterns: shafts bored straight up to the surface and capped with shielded glass, so that every few hundred paces you passed under a well of light and looked up, and there at the top of it, small and banded and impossibly far, was Jupiter. Sol stopped under the first lantern, as he always did. The planet hung in its circle of glass like an eye. Pell stopped beside him and looked up too, politely, because Sol was looking.

When Sol looked down again, the porters and their cart had gone on out of sight along the gallery, and Pell was standing a little apart with the patient face he wore through long services. “Your Grace?” Sol asked him how long they had been standing there. Some minutes, Pell said, and smiled; His Grace did love the lanterns, didn’t he? Sol agreed that he did. It was true. He did not remember the minutes at all.

The gravity was the thing one had to remember. On Mars a man weighed a little more than a third of himself; on Europa he weighed almost nothing, and every step wanted to become a leap. The colonists wore weighted boots and walked with a long gliding shuffle, and newcomers could be picked out at once, bobbing along the gallery like corks. Sol had learned the shuffle three centuries ago, and his body remembered it before he did.

The Mercy Office’s holding house stood at the end of a side gallery where the ice had been faced with white stone. There was no sign over the door. There did not need to be. It opened before they reached it, and a woman in white came out to meet them with both hands held out.

“Your Grace. You’re very welcome. I’m Imogen Sallow; I have the house.” She was tall, with a long calm face and grey eyes, and she spoke in the voice all the Mercy Office spoke in, low and even and warm, the voice of a nurse at a bedside at night. “You’ll want to see him first, I expect. He’s resting. He’s been very peaceful.”
“In a moment,” Sol said. “I’d like to see the house.”
“Of course.”

He had seen holding houses on Concord and Titan and in Sion, and had always found them reassuring, and this was the best of them. It was clean the way a thing is clean when people care about it: not merely wiped but tended. The corridors were white and wide and softly lit, and the ice showed through in long panels of glass, blue and deep, with light moving far down inside it. There were no bars. The doors closed without any lock that he could see, and each had a small pane at eye height so the wardens could look in without disturbing anyone. Through one he saw a young woman sitting cross-legged on her bed, combing her hair. Through another, a man asleep with his hand under his cheek. In every room, in a small alcove, a Pearl glowed.
“They find it calming,” Sallow said. “Most of them pray a great deal while they’re with us.”
“How long are they with you?”

“A few weeks, until the Hall has a place for them. It depends on the assessment.” She walked with her hands folded in front of her. “We read them when they come in, Your Grace. Not the mind, of course. No one can read a mind. Only the pattern of it, the way it sits in the Halo. And in the infected, the pattern has a fault in it. A place the Halo can’t make sense of.” She considered. “Noise, the technicians call it. Like a wrong note held under the music.”
“And the seizures?”

“Are the fault expressing itself. The mind has grown wrong around the Halo, the way a tree grows wrong around a wire, and every so often it pulls.” She smiled at him. “The wardens have an old name for it. Bad hardware. It isn’t a judgment, you understand. It isn’t the person. It’s the wiring.” Her face grew gentle with regret. “And the wiring can’t be put right, Your Grace, not while the body lives. The noise runs all through. So we don’t try to mend them here. We let them go where they can be mended.”
“At the Hall.”

“At the Hall. They’re released.” She said it simply, the way one says that ice is cold. “A warm cup, and the cradle song, and someone holding their hand. Their own Halo carries them up into the City, and the Face finishes there what none of us could. I’ve been with the Office a hundred and forty years. I’ve never stopped thinking it’s the most merciful work there is.”

Sol believed her. He had always believed it. He had preached it at Concord and at Abundance and in the chapels of Sion: that the Virus was the last sickness left in the new creation, and the only one the Face kept back to heal with its own hand; that the infected were not wicked but wounded; that there was no shame in being carried up early, and no cruelty in the carrying. He had signed more custody orders than he could count, and he had signed every one of them with a kind of tenderness, the way he signed an ascension: one more soul sent up, gently, to the one physician who could not fail. It had never occurred to him to sign them any other way.

As they passed one door, a woman inside looked up from her bed, saw his robes, and came to the glass. She was young-faced and pale, with a healing bruise on her forehead where she must have fallen. She laid her palm flat on the pane.
“Your Grace,” she said, muffled. “When can I go home?”
“Soon,” Sol said. “Very soon.” It was what one said, and it was true; the City was home, in the end, for everyone. “What’s your name?”
“Della, Your Grace. Della Pryor. From Abundance.”
“Della,” he said, so that she would see him keep it.
She smiled and took her hand away and went back to her bed. Sallow had stopped beside him. Her face had not changed; it was as calm and kind as before.

“They all ask that, at first,” she said. “They mean their own beds. By the end of the week they’ve understood.” She looked through the pane at the young woman settling herself on the blanket. “Nobody comes home, Your Grace. They go up. Once they’ve understood that, they’re very peaceful.”
At the end of the corridor she opened the old man’s record for him in the light between their hands.

Hale, Stephen. Born: Earth. Residence: none registered. Taken: Abundance, the Bounty Market, on the report of a patron. Custody: Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. Assessment: pending. Renewal: and then, in the registry’s gentle script, the phrase it used for the denied: Gift not received.
Stephen Hale.

Sol read the name twice. It was an ordinary name. There must have been ten thousand Stephens in the inner colonies and a few hundred Hales. And yet it sat in him oddly, the way a word does that you have not used in years and suddenly find in your mouth, already shaped, before you know you meant to say it. He waited for it to become something. It did not.
“Assessment pending?”

“We’ve been letting him rest,” Sallow said. “He’s very tired. The old ones always are.” She closed the record. “He’s asked for nothing, Your Grace, except that his bag not be taken. I understood that was your instruction.”
“It was.”
“Then it’s been kept.” She touched the door, and it slid aside without a sound. “I’ll be in my office when you’re finished.”

The room was small and white, and one whole wall of it was bare ice, glowing faintly blue with the light of the gallery behind. The Pearl was in its alcove opposite. The old man was sitting on the edge of the bed with his back to it, facing the ice, his cloth bag on his knees and his spotted hands folded on top of the bag. They had dressed him in the soft white clothes of the house. In the cold blue light his face looked older than it had in the market, the hollows deeper, the skin of his throat finer and looser, and Sol saw that his hands had a small tremor in them that did not stop even when they were still.
He looked up. His eyes were clear.
“You came,” he said.
“I said I would.”
“You did.” The old man smiled. His tongue was still healing, and it thickened his words a little. “You always did what you said. It was one of the more annoying things about you.”
Sol let that pass. He drew the room’s one chair away from the wall and sat. In the low gravity it barely took his weight. “Are you comfortable? Are they treating you well?”
“Very well. They’re very kind. Everyone here is very kind.” The smile turned wry. “I don’t think I’ve ever been treated so kindly in my life.”
“I wanted to tell you myself what will happen. So that you aren’t afraid.”
“That’s good of you.”

So Sol told him. He told it the way he had told it to frightened families on a dozen worlds: the assessment, which was only a reading and did not hurt; a few quiet weeks here; and then the Hall, and the release, which was the gentlest rite the church had. A warm cup, and the cradle song, and a hand held. The Halo that had kept him alive through every crossing he had ever made would carry him up one last time, into the City of the Throne, and there the Face would mend what no one on any world could mend, and he would be whole, and young, and free of the seizures for good. He told it well. He had always been able to make the doctrine sound like what it was, a kindness. The old man listened without interrupting, his head a little on one side, with an expression Sol could not quite read. It was the look of someone listening to a child explain, very earnestly, a thing the child has only just learned.
“And then the City,” Stephen said, when he had finished.
“Yes.”
“Home.” The old man tried the word as if it were a coat someone had lent him.
“For all of us, in the end.”
“That’s kind.” He looked down at his hands. “I won’t be renewed.”
“I know you’ve refused it before. I understand that there may have been reasons...”
“I haven’t refused it. I’ve just told you a fact.” He said it gently, almost apologetically. “I won’t be renewed.”
“It doesn’t matter now. It’s only a few weeks, and in the City...”

He stopped. He had been about to say in the City you’ll be young again, and he heard, before he said it, what the sentence stepped over. Left to himself, the old man would go on as he was. He would go on getting older, his hands shaking a little more each season, his skin loosening, his hair thinning, until one day he would simply stop, as people had stopped in the old world. Sol had known that, in the way one knows a fact in a book. He had never once sat in a chair across from it. The release would spare this man that. He held on to the thought. It was exactly what the word mercy was for.
“You won’t come to that,” he said. “That’s the mercy of it.”
“Won’t I?” Stephen raised his eyes. “Don’t trouble yourself over it, Sol. Truly. It’s not the worst thing.”

Sol did not know what to say to that, so he said nothing. The silence of Serenity came into the room and sat with them. Somewhere deep in the ice wall there was a long, low tick, the sound the ice made as it settled, like a great house shifting in its sleep.
“You called me by my name,” Sol said at last. “In the market.”
“I did.”
“Why?”
“Because it’s your name.” The old man seemed to consider how to go on, and then decided to go on simply. “We knew each other once.”

Sol had expected it, and still it moved through him strangely, like the name on the record. He set it aside, as he had set the name aside, and leaned forward with his elbows on his knees, the way he leaned toward the bereaved.
“I don’t think so,” he said gently.
“No. You wouldn’t.”

“It’s not uncommon, you know. After a seizure the mind reaches for something to hold on to. A face, a name. It builds a bridge out of whatever is nearest. You saw a bishop. Perhaps someone had told you my name once, years ago, and your mind...”
“Built a bridge,” Stephen said. “That’s well put. You always did put things well.”
“I have worn this face since the Judgment. I’ve held the same office, kept the same friends. I would remember.”
“Would you?”

It was asked without any edge at all. It was asked the way one asks a real question, wanting to know. The ice ticked again in the wall. Behind the old man’s shoulder the Pearl in its alcove went grey: not dim, but grey, flat as ash, for no longer than a heartbeat. Then it was gold again. Stephen did not turn round. Old relays, Sol thought, ice in the lines. He found that he had an answer ready, and that the answer was yes, and that it was taking him a moment longer than it should have to say it.
“Yes,” he said.
The old man nodded slowly, like a man conceding a point in a game he had not much minded losing. “Then it’s a delusion.”
“I think it is. And I think it’s a symptom, and that it can be healed, and that you’ll be glad of it afterward.” Sol said it kindly, because he meant it kindly. “You’ll be at peace.”
On the shelf by the bed stood the tray from the morning meal: the bread gone, the cup empty, and an orange untouched in the middle of the plate. Stephen saw him look at it.
“They bring me one every time.” He lifted his hands from the bag and let Sol watch them shake. “I can’t get into them anymore. Would you?”

It was a small thing, and Sol had done smaller for the dying. He took the orange from the plate. It was cold from the ice and heavy for its size, and the smell came up off the skin at once, sharp and wet, and he breathed through his mouth, as he always did.
“Do you still peel them in one long curl?” Stephen said.
Sol’s thumb had already found its way under the skin. He stopped.

He did. He peeled them for children at the feasts after a haloing, because the children laughed to see it: the whole skin lifted off in a single spiral that never broke, held up dangling like a spring. Then he gave the fruit away and went and washed the smell from his hands. He had never seen anyone else do it. He had never wondered where he had learned it. It was only a thing his hands knew, as they had known the valve under the fountain in the square at Abundance, and what to do on the floor of the market.

In the market it had been the scar. Now this. Each by itself was nothing; a trick done at a hundred feasts was no secret, and stories about bishops went round. He turned the fruit in his fingers, and the peel came away as it always did, in one long piece that hung down over his wrist and did not break, and he laid the bare orange in the old man’s shaking hands.
“Yes,” Stephen said. He was looking at the curl, not the fruit. “Like that.”
“You’re kind, Sol. You were always kind. People forget that about you.”

The pressure had come back behind Sol’s left eye while they talked, so quietly that he had not noticed it arrive. He found that he had raised two fingers to his brow without deciding to. He lowered them. The old man was watching him with an expression that was not wry at all.
“You should have that looked at,” Stephen said.
“It’s the light.”
Stephen glanced at the soft white ceiling, and then at the blue ice, and then back at Sol, and said nothing.
“You have your back to the Pearl,” Sol said, to say something else.
“Yes.”
“Wouldn’t you rather face it? The wardens say it helps.”
“I’d rather look at the ice.” The old man turned his head toward it. The blue light lay along his cheek. “It’s honest. It’s exactly what it looks like, all the way down.”

Sol’s eyes went to the bag on his knees. It was a plain thing of undyed cloth, worn soft, with a drawstring, and it sat on the old man’s lap with an odd heaviness, as if it held more than it should. Stephen had eaten two pieces of the orange, slowly, and set the rest back on the tray, and his hands had gone straight back to the bag.
“What do you keep in there?”
“Old things,” Stephen said, and his hands stayed where they were.
Sol stood. “If you need anything, ask the wardens. They’ll send for me.”
“You’ll come back.”
“If you’d like.”

“I would. Not today, I think. Today you’ve got your failures.” When Sol looked at him, he smiled. “Everyone knows why the bishop is in the colonies, Sol. Even the denied hear things.” He was quiet a moment. “Come back when you’re tired of tidy answers.”

Sol stood very still. It was only a phrase. People said it; in Sion it was very nearly his name. Aurelian had said it two nights before, on the other side of the solar system, through the relay of Sion, and it meant nothing that a sick old man under the ice of Europa had said it too. He nodded, and touched the door, and it opened.
“Sol.”
He turned.
“It’s good to see you,” Stephen said. He said it plainly, warmly, as one says it to a friend at the end of a long absence, and then he turned back to the ice.
Sallow’s office was a small white room with a single panel of ice for a wall and a desk with nothing on it. She rose when he came in.
“I’m here about the ascension failures as well,” Sol said. “There have been five on Serenity. I’d like to know whether any of them passed through this house. Families, witnesses, anyone.”
“I’ll check, Your Grace, but I’d be surprised.” She opened the ledger between them, and the house’s records rose into the light in long, orderly rows. “We keep everything. You’re welcome to it.”

Each row held a name and a face, an origin, a date of intake. There was a column for the witness who had made the report: a neighbor, a coworker, her husband, his daughter, a patron. There was a column for the assessment, and in nearly every row it read noise confirmed. There was a column for the transfer to the Hall. And there was a final column, filled in afterward in the Hall’s own hand, and in every row the final column read the same.
Released.

Forty-one rows this year. Sol let the ledger run back. Last year: thirty-eight, and every one of them released. The year before. Ten years before. The column ran down through the decades in a single unbroken line of gentle script, and it was some time before he understood what was bothering him about it, and when he understood, it was not a thing in the ledger. It was a thing that was not in it.

He had presided over ascensions for four hundred years, and every one that went through had come back with the same word on it, the word the clerk’s hand came down on in every cathedral in the worlds. Received. It was not here. Not once, in forty-one rows or in four thousand. Released, and after it nothing at all.
“None of your five are here, Your Grace,” Sallow said. “I’m sorry.”
“They’re never received,” Sol said. “Only released.”

“No.” She did not seem surprised by the question. “Mercy has its own rite, Your Grace. It isn’t an ordinary ascension. They don’t go up through a cathedral and a clerk and a gate; they’re too ill for that, and the noise would go with them. The Hall releases them, and the Face takes them in by its own door. It doesn’t send word back to a holding house.” She smiled. “We’re told what we need to be told.”
“And the families?”
“Are told their loved ones are in Mercy. Resting. Their Pearls show a resting light until the Face has finished with them. They’re very comforted by it.”
Sol thought of the pale light on the garden ring at Abundance, and the family eating their breakfast facing it, and the place they had laid. “Has anyone ever visited one? Afterward, in the City?”
He asked it lightly. She smiled at him with perfect patience.
“They’re resting, Your Grace. They can’t receive yet. The families understand.”

He had answered it the same way himself, three days ago, walking on with cake on his fingers. Healing took the time it took. He stood looking at the long column of names, running back down the decades, a hundred years of them and then two, every one of them still resting, and he did not let himself ask how long a time that was. The noise ran all through a mind, Sallow had said, and the Face did not hurry; a thing so deep was not mended in a season, or in ten. One did not go calling on a friend in the middle of surgery. The resting light was the healing, and the families saw it every evening and were glad of it, and nothing in it needed a bishop at all. That was the whole beauty of it.
He was still standing there when Pell came in, a little out of breath from hurrying in boots that were not heavy enough.

“Your Grace. Forgive me. The infirmary in the lower workings has asked for you. There’s been a fall of ice in the north shafts, and one of the drill crew is badly hurt. They don’t expect him to last the afternoon.” Pell lowered his voice. “The chaplain asks whether you would preside. Given the failures, he says. He would rather it were you.”
“I’ll come now,” Sol said, and even then, with the ledger hanging open behind him, some small unworthy part of him was glad to have been asked for.

He followed Pell out into the white corridor. Behind him, in the warden’s quiet office, the ledger still hung open in the light above the empty desk, forty-one names long this year, every line ending in the same place.
